A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same fairness-aware graph-bandit framework and advertising application. All 17 pages of v1 and 15 pages of v2, including their figures, equations and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 2–3 report original advertising-allocation experiments with fixed and time-varying feedback graphs, averaged over five trials.

after.justification: Section 6 and Figures 2–3 report original experiments under empty, fixed and time-varying feedback graphs, averaged over 30 trials.

M1.justification: The reward changes from state-dependent revenue plus explicitly weighted fairness terms in v1 Equation 4 to immediate action income minus penalties in v2 Equation 2. The exploration LP also changes from outgoing-neighbor sums to incoming feedback-edge sums. These affect the objective and action selection, beyond consolidating the existing algorithms.

E1.justification: The advertising-allocation task and underlying revenue-data source remain the same; the Lu/Balseiro citations refer to the same titled work. v2 adds an empty-graph scenario with no side observations, extending the evaluated feedback conditions.

E2.justification: Figures 2–3 add an empty-graph, bandit-only version of the algorithm as an evaluated baseline. The dynamic and fixed-action hindsight benchmarks remain. The methods surveyed in Table 1 are not additional experimentally evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: Section 6 changes from three advertisers with fixed target shares to five with Dirichlet-sampled targets. Random learning-rate/confidence choices become eta = 1/15 and delta = 0.025, and horizons extend from 30–70 to 30–80. The stated graph-generation rule changes from a maximum-acyclic-subgraph restriction to per-edge inclusion probability 0.8.

E4.justification: The added empty-graph control tests whether side observations improve performance, a question not isolated by v1's fixed-versus-changing graph comparison. No broader robustness or sensitivity study is added.

E5.justification: The reported number of trials per horizon increases from five to 30. Both versions display means with plus/minus one standard deviation; v2 does not introduce confidence intervals, significance tests or seed reporting.

E6.justification: Figures 2–3 replace the experimental curves and add empty-graph outcomes and longer horizons. v1 shows negative reward curves, whereas v2 shows positive curves under its revised reward and data settings. v2 reports worse baseline regret and slightly better time-varying than fixed-graph performance; these are not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The weak-regret rate and appendix proof are substantially retained. v2 explicitly assumes bounded rewards, specifies the action-only graph in the theorem's maximum-acyclic-subgraph term, and corrects v1's exchanged bandit/expert regret statements. These refine existing theory rather than provide a new proof.

C1.justification: The retitled paper and explicit contribution list retain the central claims: representing multiple evolving fairness objectives through graph-structured partial feedback and applying a bandit algorithm with a weak-regret guarantee. Fairness-regularizer vertices and support for changing graphs were already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking performance differences to available feedback and attributing dynamic-benchmark variability to its larger integer program. It also interprets graph complexity, but newly claims that larger mas means more informative feedback, contradicting its own complete-graph and empty-graph examples.

D1.justification: v1 refers to supplementary implementation material and promises public release after acceptance. v2 supplies a public implementation-and-experiment repository address and substantially more reproducibility information, including income normalization, target-share sampling and explicit edge generation. These are documented access instructions and details; the repository was not inspected.

R1.justification: The core fairness-resolution and graph-bandit antecedents remain. v2 adds references including Kozdoba et al., Lai and Robbins, and Diamond and Boyd, introduces an explicit contrast with MDP approaches, and removes the PSPACE critique and several optimization and political-advertising references. Much fairness background was already in v1's appendix.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, framework exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Appendix fairness discussions move into the main related-work section, notation is simplified, and the separate fixed/changing-graph algorithm presentations are consolidated. The appendix is reduced to the retained proof.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a journal layout with redesigned front matter and running headers. Figures 2–3 expand from two to three panels with revised axes, legends and captions. The notation table is shortened and moved into Section 3, and the two algorithm displays are consolidated.

improvement.justification: The empty-graph control directly tests the value of side feedback, while clearer experimental instructions and reported code access improve reproducibility. Correcting the LP edge direction and bandit/expert regret statements also helps. These gains are tempered by new errors: Table 2 reverses the hindsight-benchmark descriptions, and the graph-information interpretation contradicts its own examples. The overall improvement is therefore limited.
